Pathway

Curriculum & ELA

For Core ELA and K–12 curriculum development roles. Ten minutes with these three samples shows how I write texts, units and assessments for Grades 3–5.

Open these first

  1. WS2 · Six original texts. Read "The Crunching Sound" and its analysis: it shows why a text can belong in Grade 4 when its readability formula says Grade 2.
  2. WS1 · Grade 4 unit. Look at the knowledge progression, then Lesson 3, where students first integrate two texts.
  3. WS6 · Assessment. Look at the distractor rationales: each wrong answer names the misunderstanding it catches.
WS2 Representative sample

Six Original Texts for Grades 3–5

New passages, each with its complexity analysis shown.

Six original literary and informational texts for readers in Grades 3–5, several set in The Bahamas. Each comes with a qualitative analysis, a quantitative readability estimate, and reader-and-task notes explaining where it fits and why. It shows writing for young readers and the judgment behind placing a text in a grade band, without relying on a single score.

Original texts · Text complexity · Literary and informational · Culturally relevantOpen WS2 →WS1 Representative sample

Nature's Engineers: A Grade 4 Knowledge-Building Unit

How do beavers, termites and coral change the places they live?

A Grade 4 unit built on a sequenced text set about animals that reshape their environments. Students build knowledge text by text, read closely, discuss, and write an explanatory piece that cites evidence. Includes the unit plan, knowledge progression, five fully written lessons, a culminating task with rubric, and a rights log for every text. All texts are original.

Knowledge-building units · Text sets · Comprehension · PermissionsOpen WS1 →WS6 Representative sample

Measuring What the Unit Teaches: Assessment and Rubrics

Every item mapped to a standard, every wrong answer explained.

An end-of-unit assessment for Nature's Engineers: a blueprint, 22 items across selected-response, evidence-based and constructed-response formats, answer keys, distractor rationales, scoring rubrics and an item review checklist. It shows how each item measures the standard it claims, what each wrong answer reveals, and how teachers can read the results.
